preamble: The Modern South Arabian languages keep the Proto-Semitic emphatic lateral *ṣ́ as a lateral fricative, the counterpart of Arabic ḍād ض. It is usually given as an ejective [ɬʼ] (Wikipedia, Modern South Arabian; Brewster 2021: 32, cited by Wikipedia), but in some descriptions it is pharyngealized [ɬˤ]: glottalization gives way to pharyngealization. The pharyngealized lateral is not always fully voiceless: Wikipedia's Mehri article makes emphatic fricatives partially voiced outside pre-pausal position (its table gives ɬ̬ˁ ~ ɬ̠ʼ), Wikipedia's Shehri article says emphatics are usually partially voiced when not glottalized, and Harsusi /ɬˤ/ is frequently voiced [ɮˤ] between vowels (Wikipedia, Ḥarsusi language). Watson & Al-Azraqi (2011: 430), on the other hand, describe the Gabgabat Mehri sound as voiceless. In Harsusi the phoneme is /ɬˤ/ (Al Balushi 2019: 18, 28, 49, cited by Wikipedia), and Wikipedia (Ḍād), citing Rubin 2014: 81, 109, transcribes Jibbali forms with [ɬˤ], although Wikipedia's Shehri consonant table gives glottalized ɬˀ ~ ɬʼ and says the emphatics may be ejective or pharyngealized depending on variety, speaker and phonological environment. Mehri emphatics 'may also be pharyngealized, as in Arabic' (Watson & Bellem 2011, cited by Wikipedia; compare Watson & Bellem 2010); Wikipedia's Mehri article makes them ejective before a pause and, in other positions, pharyngealized. Watson & Al-Azraqi (2011: 425–426) report the emphatic lateral as 'a pharyngealized lateralized fricative in some dialects', including that of their speaker from near Salālah, and 'an emphatic lateral sonorant in others'. The Mehri of Hawf has a voiced variant and the Mehri of Ndēd a lateral sonorant (2011: 429–430), neither of which fits this cell. The Proto-Semitic ejective is a reconstruction (Cantineau 1952; Kogan 2011: 61, cited by Wikipedia), and Wikipedia (Mehri language) suggests that Mehri may attest a transition from ejective to pharyngealized emphatics.

examples.note: Wiktionary. ẑ is Harsusi's only emphatic lateral, /ɬˤ/ in Al Balushi's table (2019: 18, cited by Wikipedia).

languageExamples.context: Emphatics are ejective or pharyngealized depending on variety, speaker and phonological environment, and usually partially voiced when not glottalized (Wikipedia, Shehri language)

examples.note: Transcription from Wikipedia (Ḍād), citing Rubin (2014: 81, 109); Wiktionary writes mírẓ̂. Wikipedia's Shehri table gives the phoneme as ɬˀ ~ ɬʼ, usually affricated.
Transcription from Wikipedia (Ḍād), citing Rubin (2014); Wiktionary writes ʾɛrẓ̂.

languageExamples.context: Positional rule (Wikipedia, Mehri language): emphatics are ejective before a pause and pharyngealized elsewhere, where emphatic fricatives are partially voiced. Watson & Al-Azraqi (2011) describe variation between dialects instead: a pharyngealized lateralized fricative for their Gabgabat speaker near Salālah (pp. 425–426), described more closely as voiceless with slight affrication (p. 430), a voiced variant in Hawf and mainly a lateral sonorant in Ndēd (pp. 429–430)

examples.to: ṣ́abb 'it became warm [water]', with a pharyngealized lateralized fricative
examples.note: Minimal set with sibb 'to insult', šubb 'be off [dog]' and śibb 'he climbed' (Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 426).

examples.to: aɬaḥūk min hāśan 'what's the laughing for?'
examples.note: Watson & Al-Azraqi (2011: 430), who describe the Gabgabat sound as 'a voiceless lateral dental fricative, with slight affrication'.
